1 Introduction

1.1 Motivation

This document extends the ACTG175 benefit-search simulation framework from survival outcomes (time-to-event) to a binary endpoint: whether a patient’s CD4 count improved from baseline to 20 weeks. The outcome is encoded on the improvement scale: \(y\_binary = I(\text{cd420} > \text{cd40})\), where a 1 indicates improvement. Combined with treatment switching (ddI \(\to\) treat = 1, ZDV+ddI \(\to\) treat = 0), \(\text{OR} > c_1\) in the analysis means ddI increases the odds of improvement in the identified subgroup — equivalently, ZDV+ddI harms improvement there. ForestSearch identifies this as a harm subgroup; subgroup_notation = "benefit" relabels it for display.

A full reference table of effect-measure / outcome-direction combinations appears in the Appendix. Section 1.3 summarises the row that applies to this vignette.

The simulation uses the forestsearch GLM simulation suite (generate_glm_dgm, calibrate_glm_interaction, simulate_from_glm_dgm) and routes through run_simulation_analysis() via class-based dispatch on the "glm_dgm" object.

1.2 Realistic Analysis Setting

A prior version of this simulation discretised every continuous covariate into a binary factor before handing the data to forestsearch() / grf.subg.harm.glm(). The binarisation used the same cuts that define the true subgroup \(Q\) (e.g. age > 34, preanti \(\leq\) 744.5). That setup implicitly gives the analysis method knowledge of the true cutpoints, which is unrealistic.

The current setup retains continuous covariates in their raw form for the analysis step. The data-generating mechanism (DGM) is built from the discretised factors (z1–z12) because generate_glm_dgm() requires factor covariates and the true subgroup must be defined algebraically. The analysis methods, however, see the raw continuous columns (age, preanti, wtkg, karnof, cd40, cd80) along with the six truly binary indicators (hemo, homo, drugs, race, gender, symptom). Cutpoints for the continuous covariates are discovered by the search methods themselves (median splits, GRF-derived cuts, policy-tree splits), exactly as in a real analysis.

ImportantWhat changes vs the prior (discretised) setup
  • Ground truth is unchanged: the true benefit subgroup \(Q\) is still \(\{\text{age} > 34\} \cap \{\text{preanti} \leq 744.5\}\) with prevalence \(\approx 34\%\), and the DGM’s OR(Q) calibration is untouched.
  • Classification metrics are unchanged in definition: flag_harm is computed identically from z1 and z2.
  • What changes is the search problem: ForestSearch must discover the cuts from candidate thresholds; GRF builds policy trees over raw continuous inputs. Expect lower sensitivity and PPV than the discretised setting, because the analyst does not receive oracle cuts.

Cut-set coverage for this run. ForestSearch is configured with cut_type = "default" (the package default), which generates four candidate cuts per continuous covariate: mean, median, Q1, and Q3. For the ACTG175 covariate distribution the median of age is approximately 34 and Q3 of preanti is approximately 744.5, so both true Q-defining cuts happen to fall inside the default candidate set — they are simply not privileged over the other candidates. The analyst has no oracle knowledge of which cuts matter; ForestSearch must select them based on the data. Switching to cut_type = "median" would exclude preanti’s Q3 cut from the candidate set entirely, providing a harder stress test. GRF policy trees search over all continuous thresholds internally and are unaffected by this setting.

1.3 Statistical Goals

This simulation study addresses three questions about ForestSearch and GRF standalone subgroup identification applied to binary outcomes in the realistic (raw covariate) setting:

  1. Detection power (H1): When a benefit subgroup \(Q\) exists with \(\text{OR}(Q) = 2\) – i.e., in \(Q\), the experimental treatment (ZDV+ddI) doubles the odds of improvement compared to ddI – how often do ForestSearch and GRF identify any subgroup?
  2. False positive control (H0): When the treatment effect is homogeneous (no true \(Q\)), how often does each method falsely declare a benefit subgroup?
  3. Classification accuracy (H1): Conditional on detection, how well does the estimated \(\hat{Q}\) recover the true \(Q\)? Measured by sensitivity (\(\text{sens}(\hat{Q})\): fraction of true \(Q\) captured) and positive predictive value (\(\text{ppv}(\hat{Q})\): fraction of \(\hat{Q}\) truly in \(Q\)).

1.4 Simulation Pipeline

The simulation proceeds in six steps:

  1. Data preparation (Section 3): Load the ACTG175 trial, restrict to arms 1 (ZDV+ddI) and 3 (ddI), switch treatment labels so ddI = treat = 1 and ZDV+ddI = treat = 0 (benefit search convention), and construct BOTH:

    1. the binary z1–z12 factor set needed by the DGM; and
    2. the realistic analysis candidate set (age, preanti, wtkg, karnof, cd40, cd80, hemo, homo, drugs, race, gender, symptom).

  2. DGM construction (Section 4): Fit a logistic regression to the observed data using the z1–z12 factor formulation, create a 5,000-subject super-population, and define the true benefit subgroup \(Q = \{z_1 = 1 \cap z_2 = 1\}\) (age > 34 AND preanti \(\leq\) 744.5). The super- population retains the raw covariate columns as well as the z1–z12 indicators.

  3. Calibration (Section 4.2): Search over k_inter values to find the interaction strength that produces \(\text{OR}(Q) = 2\) – a 2\(\times\) odds-ratio of improvement for the experimental treatment in \(Q\) (see Section 1.3 for the directional convention).

  4. Single-data analysis (Section 5): Run ForestSearch and GRF on the observed ACTG175 data using the raw analysis candidate set to verify the pipeline produces valid results before scaling to simulation.

  5. Monte Carlo simulation (Section 7): For each of 200 alternative and 200 null replicates, draw a random sample of \(N = 1000\) from the DGM super-population, run ForestSearch and GRF on the raw analysis covariates, and record detection, classification, and effect estimates.

  6. Evaluation (Section 8): Compute operating characteristics (detection, sensitivity, PPV, effect estimation bias) under both hypotheses.

1.5 Benefit Search on the OR Scale

The benefit-search approach from Leon et al. (2024, Section 4.2) applies identically to binary outcomes, with odds ratios (OR) replacing hazard ratios (HR). The full configuration is shown in the directional table in Section 1.3 and in the master reference table in Section 12; in brief, the combination of switched treatment and adverse-coded y_binary makes the package’s harm-search machinery point at the benefit direction, with screening threshold \(c_1 =\) 1.667 and consistency threshold \(c_2 =\) 1.333 (both sourced from the Quarto setup chunk). Inversion to the original scale is handled automatically by the package when subgroup_notation = "benefit" is passed to the reporting functions.

1.6 Candidate Selection: sg_focus = "maxSG"

When several candidate subgroups simultaneously meet both the screening threshold (\(c_1 =\) 1.667) and the consistency threshold (\(c_2 =\) 1.333), forestsearch() must pick one. That choice is governed by sg_focus. Five options are available:

sg_focus Primary sort Secondary Interpretation
"hr" Pcons effect Package default. Favours most-consistent candidate.
"maxSG" N Pcons Largest qualifying candidate.
"minSG" N Pcons Smallest qualifying candidate.
"hrMaxSG" N effect Compound. Forces stop_threshold = NULL.
"hrMinSG" N effect Compound. Forces stop_threshold = NULL.

For the ACTG175 benefit search, the analytic goal is to recover the largest subgroup in which the ZDV+ddI combination is superior to ddI monotherapy — the population we would, in a real trial, most want to describe and quantify. Once the screening-plus-consistency filter has passed, there is no further reason to pick a smaller, tighter subgroup; the largest qualifying candidate is the most policy-relevant one.

We therefore use fs_sg_focus <- "maxSG" throughout this document (set in the Quarto setup chunk). The concrete effect is:

  • Sort is by candidate N (descending), with Pcons as tiebreaker. Among candidates that pass screening and consistency, FS keeps the one with the largest \(|H|\).
  • Single sort criterion, so early stopping remains valid; stop_threshold can still be set if desired. (In this document we set stop_threshold = NULL so all qualifying candidates are enumerated.)

This choice has two practical consequences that we track throughout the operating-characteristics analysis:

  1. \(\widehat{|H|}\) will typically be closer to \(|Q|\) than under the default sg_focus = "hr", which trades size for consistency and tends to return strict subsets of \(Q\).
  2. The distribution of identified subgroups across simulations (reported in Section 8.2) should concentrate on a small number of definitions close to the true \(Q\) anchor, rather than fragmenting into many small tight splits.

2 GRF Standalone: Calibration Notes

The standalone GRF analysis uses grf.subg.harm.glm() with causal_forest() for candidate variable screening and policy trees for subgroup identification. The key tuning parameter is dmin.grf, the minimum absolute CATE (conditional average treatment effect) on the risk difference scale required for a policy-tree node to be valid.

2.1 Configuration

For the benefit + positive scenario with switched treatment (the ACTG175 binary configuration), the correct GRF setup is:

  • adverse_outcome = FALSE (Y = improvement is positive)
  • Treatment indicator = switched (ddI = 1, ZDV+ddI = 0)
  • GRF identifies the subgroup where the switched “treatment” produces the most negative CATE — i.e., where ddI monotherapy is worst relative to combination, which is the benefit subgroup on the original scale.

2.2 Impact of Raw Continuous Inputs on Calibration

Prior dmin.grf calibration (in grf_dmin_calibration_binary.qmd) was conducted on discretised inputs (z1–z12 binary factors) and recommended dmin.grf = 0.02 for the benefit + positive binary configuration.

With raw continuous inputs the policy-tree search evaluates many more candidate thresholds per covariate, which tends to:

  • Widen the null distribution of the best CATE, inflating the false positive rate at a given dmin.grf.
  • Improve sensitivity to the true cuts when they align with natural splits in the covariate distribution.

The current document uses dmin.grf = 0.1 as a conservative default carried over from the discretised setting. A dedicated calibration run with raw continuous inputs is recommended before production scaling.

Note

The GRF FPR is higher than ForestSearch’s because GRF lacks the bootstrap consistency filter. ForestSearch requires the subgroup effect to exceed a threshold in 90% of bootstrap replicates, providing stronger FPR control at the cost of lower detection. The two methods are complementary: GRF provides a threshold-free comparison.

# forestsearch v0.2.0 via the exported helpers collect_results() and

Data preparation (click to expand) 
t0 <- proc.time()[3]

# -- ACTG175: arms 1 (ZDV+ddI) vs 3 (ddI) ------------------------------------
actg_df <- subset(speff2trial::ACTG175, arms %in% actg_arms)
actg_df$id <- seq_len(nrow(actg_df))

# Original treatment: arm 1 = 1, arm 3 = 0
actg_df$treat_orig <- ifelse(actg_df$arms == actg_treat_arm, 1L, 0L)

# Switched treatment for benefit search
actg_df$treat <- 1L - actg_df$treat_orig

# -- Binary outcome: CD4 response at 20 weeks ---------------------------------
# Improvement scale: y_binary = 1 when the patient's CD4 count improved
# (cd420 > cd40).  With switched treatment (ddI = 1), OR > c1 in Q means
# ddI increases the odds of improvement — ForestSearch identifies this as
# the "harm" subgroup; subgroup_notation = "benefit" relabels for display.
actg_df$y_binary <- as.integer(actg_df$cd420 > actg_df$cd40)

# Remove subjects with missing cd420
n_before <- nrow(actg_df)
actg_df <- actg_df[!is.na(actg_df$cd420), ]
n_after  <- nrow(actg_df)

# =============================================================================
# Two parallel covariate views are constructed on the SAME data frame:
#
#   (1) DGM factor set: z1--z12 binary factors. Used by generate_glm_dgm()
#       and calibrate_glm_interaction() to fit the baseline logistic
#       regression and define the TRUE subgroup Q = {z1=1 & z2=1}.
#
#   (2) Analysis candidate set: raw continuous covariates + truly binary
#       indicators. Used by forestsearch() and grf.subg.harm.glm() in
#       both the observed-data analysis and every simulated replicate.
#       The analyst does NOT know the cuts that define Q.
# =============================================================================

# -- (1) DGM factor set: z1-z12 binary factors --------------------------------
#
# The z-series preserves the discretisation from León et al. (2024,
# Section 4.2). These are needed by the DGM because generate_glm_dgm()
# requires factor covariates, and because the true Q is defined
# algebraically in terms of z1 and z2.
actg_df$z1  <- as.factor(ifelse(actg_df$age > actg_age_cut, 1L, 0L))
actg_df$z2  <- as.factor(ifelse(actg_df$preanti <= actg_preanti_cut, 1L, 0L))
actg_df$z3  <- as.factor(ifelse(actg_df$wtkg <= 75, 1L, 0L))
actg_df$z4  <- as.factor(ifelse(
  actg_df$karnof <= median(actg_df$karnof), 1L, 0L))
actg_df$z5  <- as.factor(ifelse(
  actg_df$cd40 <= median(actg_df$cd40), 1L, 0L))
actg_df$z6  <- as.factor(ifelse(
  actg_df$cd80 <= median(actg_df$cd80), 1L, 0L))
actg_df$z7  <- as.factor(actg_df$hemo)
actg_df$z8  <- as.factor(actg_df$homo)
actg_df$z9  <- as.factor(actg_df$drugs)
actg_df$z10 <- as.factor(actg_df$race)
actg_df$z11 <- as.factor(actg_df$gender)
actg_df$z12 <- as.factor(actg_df$symptom)

# -- (2) Analysis candidate set: raw + binary ---------------------------------
#
# The continuous columns (age, preanti, wtkg, karnof, cd40, cd80) are
# ALREADY in the ACTG175 dataframe in their raw form. We make the six
# truly-binary indicators into factors so that forestsearch's
# is.continuous() detection treats them as categorical without
# attempting median/GRF cuts.
for (v in analysis_binary_vars) {
  actg_df[[v]] <- as.factor(actg_df[[v]])
}

confounders_analysis <- c(analysis_continuous_vars, analysis_binary_vars)

# Sanity: covariate-type inventory for the analyst-visible candidate set
cov_types <- vapply(confounders_analysis,
  function(v) if (is.factor(actg_df[[v]])) "factor" else class(actg_df[[v]])[1],
  character(1))
n_unique_per_cov <- vapply(confounders_analysis,
  function(v) length(unique(actg_df[[v]])), integer(1))

# -- True subgroup flag (for reference; generate_glm_dgm creates its own) -----
actg_df$flag_harm_ref <- as.integer(
  actg_df$z1 == 1 & actg_df$z2 == 1
)

# -- Summary scalars captured for downstream display ---------------------------
# y_binary = improvement: mean(y_binary) is the improvement rate directly.
n_ex_missing <- n_before - n_after
resp_overall <- 100 * mean(actg_df$y_binary)
resp_ZDV_ddI <- 100 * mean(actg_df$y_binary[actg_df$treat_orig == 1])
resp_ddI     <- 100 * mean(actg_df$y_binary[actg_df$treat_orig == 0])
Q_n          <- sum(actg_df$flag_harm_ref)
Q_N          <- nrow(actg_df)
Q_prev_pct   <- 100 * mean(actg_df$flag_harm_ref)

# Response-rate 2x2 grid (row = subgroup, col = treatment arm)
resp_grid <- data.frame(
  Subgroup  = c("Q (age > 34 & preanti \u2264 745)",
                "Qc (complement)"),
  `ZDV+ddI` = c(
    100 * mean(actg_df$y_binary[actg_df$flag_harm_ref == 1 & actg_df$treat_orig == 1]),
    100 * mean(actg_df$y_binary[actg_df$flag_harm_ref == 0 & actg_df$treat_orig == 1])),
  `ddI`     = c(
    100 * mean(actg_df$y_binary[actg_df$flag_harm_ref == 1 & actg_df$treat_orig == 0]),
    100 * mean(actg_df$y_binary[actg_df$flag_harm_ref == 0 & actg_df$treat_orig == 0])),
  check.names = FALSE
)

timings$data_prep <- proc.time()[3] - t0
NoteDataset summary
  • Source cohort: ACTG175 arms 1 (ZDV+ddI, experimental) and 3 (ddI, control). N = 1083 before exclusion, N = 1083 after removing 0 subject(s) with missing cd420.
  • Outcome: binary response, y_binary = I(cd420 > cd40) (improvement scale). Overall improvement rate 60.3%; ZDV+ddI arm 65.3%; ddI arm 55.6%.
  • True subgroup Q (used for ground-truth classification only, not exposed to the analysis methods): age \(>\) 34 AND preanti \(\le\) 744.5. Prevalence 382 / 1083 (35.3%).
  • Analysis candidate set (12 covariates): 6 continuous (age, preanti, wtkg, karnof, cd40, cd80) + 6 binary factors (hemo, homo, drugs, race, gender, symptom).
  • DGM factor set: z1–z12 binary factors, preserving the discretisation from León et al. (2024, Section 4.2). Kept on the same data frame so generate_glm_dgm() can build the super-population from the factor representation while the analysis methods see the raw continuous covariates.

4 Creating the Binary DGM

The GLM DGM uses generate_glm_dgm() to fit a logistic regression on the observed ACTG175 data, create a super-population with individual-level potential outcomes (\(p_0\), \(p_1\)), and compute true subgroup effects. calibrate_glm_interaction() then searches for the k_inter that produces the target OR(Q).

Note on DGM inputs. The DGM continues to use the z1–z12 factor formulation. This is a design requirement of generate_glm_dgm() (which coerces any input to factor via as.factor()) and is also the natural way to define the true subgroup \(Q\) algebraically. The super-population returned by the DGM retains all original columns of actg_df, including the raw age, preanti, wtkg, karnof, cd40, cd80 columns, which are then used by the analysis step.

4.1 Step 1: Build Initial DGM

Show code 
t0 <- proc.time()[3]

dgm_alt_init <- generate_glm_dgm(
  data          = actg_df,
  factor_vars   = dgm_factor_vars,
  outcome_var   = "y_binary",
  treatment_var = "treat",
  outcome_type  = "binary",
  effect_measure = "OR",
  subgroup_vars = dgm_subgroup_vars,
  subgroup_cuts = dgm_subgroup_cuts,
  model         = "alt",
  k_treat       = dgm_k_treat_alt,

)

4.2 Step 2: Calibrate for Target OR

4.2.1 Why calibrate?

The DGM’s k_inter parameter controls the strength of the treatment-by-subgroup interaction on the log-odds scale. Because the mapping from k_inter to the marginal OR(Q) is non-linear and depends on the covariate distribution and baseline response rates, we search over a grid of candidate values.

calibrate_glm_interaction() automates this process: it evaluates generate_glm_dgm() at each grid point and selects the k_inter closest to the target.

Show code 
t0 <- proc.time()[3]

dgm_calibrated <- calibrate_glm_interaction(
  data            = actg_df,
  factor_vars     = dgm_factor_vars,
  outcome_var     = "y_binary",
  treatment_var   = "treat",
  target_effect   = cal_target_or,
  outcome_type    = "binary",
  effect_measure  = "OR",
  subgroup_vars   = dgm_subgroup_vars,
  subgroup_cuts   = dgm_subgroup_cuts,
  k_treat         = dgm_k_treat_alt,
  k_inter_range   = cal_k_grid_range,
  grid_step       = cal_grid_step,
  n_super         = dgm_n_super,
  seed            = sim_seed,
  verbose         = TRUE
)

4.2.3 Illustrative k_treat values: OR(ITT), OR(Q), and gap to c1

To give the reader a concrete sense of how k_treat shifts the marginal and subgroup effects under H1, the table below holds the calibrated k_inter fixed and varies k_treat over the same grid \(\{0.5, 1.0, 1.5\}\) as the null analog. k_treat scales the fitted main treatment effect directly, so \(\text{OR}(\text{ITT})\) tracks k_treat smoothly; \(\text{OR}(Q)\) inherits both the scaled main effect and the held-fixed interaction, so it hits the calibration target \(\text{OR}(Q) = 2\) only at the calibration k_treat and drifts away as k_treat is perturbed. Larger k_treat amplifies the main effect, pushing both \(\text{OR}(\text{ITT})\) and \(\text{OR}(Q)\) further above c1 (improving FS detection); smaller k_treat attenuates and may pull \(\text{OR}(Q)\) back toward c1 (degrading detection).

Build three illustrative alt DGMs and tabulate (click to expand) 
# Three illustrative alt DGMs.  k_inter is HELD FIXED at the value
# returned by calibration (dgm_calibrated$model_params$k_inter); only
# k_treat varies.  These DGMs are NOT used in the simulation loop
# below — the simulation uses dgm_calibrated, which is the calibrated
# alt DGM at k_treat = dgm_k_treat_alt.  The grid here is purely a
# didactic table.
k_inter_cal  <- dgm_calibrated$model_params$k_inter
k_treat_grid <- c(0.5, 1.0, 1.5)

illust_rows_alt <- lapply(k_treat_grid, function(k) {
  d <- generate_glm_dgm(
    data           = actg_df,
    factor_vars    = dgm_factor_vars,
    outcome_var    = "y_binary",
    treatment_var  = "treat",
    outcome_type   = "binary",
    effect_measure = "OR",
    subgroup_vars  = dgm_subgroup_vars,
    subgroup_cuts  = dgm_subgroup_cuts,
    model          = "alt",
    k_treat        = k,
    k_inter        = k_inter_cal,
    n_super        = dgm_n_super,
    seed           = sim_seed,
    verbose        = FALSE
  )
  or_ITT_switched <- as.numeric(d$hazard_ratios$overall)
  or_Q_switched   <- as.numeric(d$hazard_ratios$harm_subgroup)
  data.frame(
    k_treat       = k,
    or_itt_switch = or_ITT_switched,
    or_itt_orig   = 1 / or_ITT_switched,
    or_Q_switch   = or_Q_switched,
    or_Q_orig     = 1 / or_Q_switched,
    gap_to_c1     = fs_or_threshold - or_Q_switched
  )
})
illust_tbl_alt <- do.call(rbind, illust_rows_alt)

gt::gt(illust_tbl_alt) |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title    = "Illustrative alt DGMs: OR(ITT), OR(Q), and gap to c1 by k_treat",
    subtitle = sprintf(
      paste0("ACTG175 benefit search, switched scale; ",
             "c1 = %.3f, k_inter = %.3f (held fixed), n_super = %d"),
      fs_or_threshold, k_inter_cal, dgm_n_super
    )
  ) |>
  gt::tab_spanner(
    label   = "OR(ITT)",
    columns = c(or_itt_switch, or_itt_orig)
  ) |>
  gt::tab_spanner(
    label   = "OR(Q)",
    columns = c(or_Q_switch, or_Q_orig)
  ) |>
  gt::cols_label(
    k_treat       = "k_treat",
    or_itt_switch = "switched",
    or_itt_orig   = "original",
    or_Q_switch   = "switched",
    or_Q_orig     = "original",
    gap_to_c1     = gt::md("Gap (c1 \u2212 OR_Q_switched)")
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns  = c(or_itt_switch, or_itt_orig,
                 or_Q_switch,   or_Q_orig,   gap_to_c1),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = k_treat, decimals = 1) |>
  gt::tab_style(
    style    = gt::cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = gt::cells_body(rows = k_treat == 1.0)
  ) |>
  gt::tab_footnote(
    footnote = paste0(
      "k_treat = 1.0 (bold row) preserves the fitted main treatment ",
      "effect; this is the function default for generate_glm_dgm(). ",
      "This document's calibration was performed at k_treat = ",
      format(dgm_k_treat_alt, nsmall = 1),
      " (set in the setup chunk via dgm_k_treat_alt), and the resulting ",
      "k_inter = ", sprintf("%.3f", k_inter_cal),
      " is held fixed across all three rows.  k_treat scales the main ",
      "treatment effect directly, so OR(ITT) tracks k_treat smoothly; ",
      "OR(Q) hits the calibration target only at the calibration k_treat ",
      "because the held-fixed k_inter still adds to the linear predictor ",
      "for Q members regardless of k_treat. ",
      "Note: under H1, a NEGATIVE gap (last column) means OR(Q) exceeds ",
      "c1, which is detection-favorable -- the opposite sign convention ",
      "from the null table (where a positive gap is favorable, i.e., no ",
      "false alarm). Effects are computed exactly from the super-",
      "population's individual potential outcomes (p0, p1); marginal ORs ",
      "depend on the covariate distribution and are not, in general, ",
      "equal to any single conditional OR."
    )
  )

This document's calibration was performed at k_treat = 1.0 (set in the setup chunk via dgm_k_treat_alt), and the resulting k_inter = 1.150 is held fixed across all three rows. k_treat scales the main treatment effect directly, so OR(ITT) tracks k_treat smoothly; OR(Q) hits the calibration target only at the calibration k_treat because the held-fixed k_inter still adds to the linear predictor for Q members regardless of k_treat. Note: under H1, a NEGATIVE gap (last column) means OR(Q) exceeds c1, which is detection-favorable -- the opposite sign convention from the null table (where a positive gap is favorable, i.e., no false alarm). Effects are computed exactly from the super-population's individual potential outcomes (p0, p1); marginal ORs depend on the covariate distribution and are not, in general, equal to any single conditional OR.

4.3 Step 3: Create Null DGM

Under model = "null", the treatment effect is homogeneous across all patients (no treatment effect heterogeneity). Per León et al. (2024, Section 3), \(Q = \emptyset\) and \(Q^c\) is the ITT population. The flag_harm column is retained as a structural label in the simulated data (marking \(z_1 = 1 \cap z_2 = 1\)) but has no treatment-effect meaning: there is no true benefit subgroup under this hypothesis.

Show code

  factor_vars   = dgm_factor_vars,
  outcome_var   = "y_binary",
  treatment_var = "treat",
  outcome_type  = "binary",
  subgroup_vars = dgm_subgroup_vars,
  subgroup_cuts = dgm_subgroup_cuts,
  model         = "null",
  k_treat       = dgm_k_treat_null,
  n_super       = dgm_n_super,
  seed          = sim_seed,
  verbose       = TRUE
)

4.3.1 Illustrative k_treat values: OR(ITT) and gap to c1

To give the reader a concrete sense of how k_treat controls the marginal ITT effect and therefore the gap from c1, the table below constructs three illustrative null DGMs at k_treat \(\in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5\}\) using the same data, factor list, super-population size, and seed as the main dgm_null above. The default (k_treat = 1.0) preserves the fitted ITT effect; larger k_treat amplifies the marginal benefit, pushing the switched-scale OR further above 1 and narrowing the gap to c1; smaller k_treat attenuates the marginal effect toward OR \(\approx 1\) and widens the gap.

5 Single-Data Analysis

ImportantReal-data setting: no ground-truth classification

This section analyses the actual ACTG175 data – not a simulated trial. The true benefit subgroup in a real trial is unknown; it is the object the analysis is trying to estimate. We therefore report the subgroup ForestSearch identifies and the resulting arm-specific ORs, but we do not compute classification metrics (sens / spec / PPV) against any reference subgroup – there is no clinical truth to classify against. Classification is only meaningful in the simulation setting of Section 7, where the DGM fixes a known \(Q\).

Before any simulation, run ForestSearch on the actual ACTG175 data with details = TRUE to examine every step of the procedure: LASSO screening, GRF variable importance, candidate enumeration, and bootstrap consistency.

The analysis uses the realistic candidate set:

Echo candidate covariate set (click to expand) 
cat("Analysis candidate covariates (no oracle cuts):\n")
cat("  Continuous:", paste(analysis_continuous_vars, collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("  Binary:    ", paste(analysis_binary_vars, collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("\nForestsearch / GRF will discover cuts on the continuous\n")
cat("covariates themselves; the TRUE cuts (age > 34, preanti <= 745)\n")
cat("are NOT provided.\n")
NoteWhat the analysis methods see

The analysis candidate set (passed to forestsearch() / grf.subg.harm.glm() as confounders.name) is:

  • Continuous (6): age, preanti, wtkg, karnof, cd40, cd80
  • Binary (6): hemo, homo, drugs, race, gender, symptom

The methods discover cuts on the continuous covariates themselves; the TRUE cuts (age \(>\) 34, preanti \(\le\) 744.5) are not provided.

fs_run() on real data (click to expand) 
t0 <- proc.time()[3]

# ForestSearch on ACTG175 observed data
#   outcome_type = 'binary', effect_measure = 'OR'
#   Treatment: switched (ddI = 1, ZDV+ddI = 0)
#   Y = I(cd420 > cd40) = improvement
#   Covariates: RAW continuous + binary indicators
#   Thresholds: c1 = fs_or_threshold, c2 = fs_or_consistency

fs_actg <- fs_run(
  data        = actg_df,
  outcome_col = "y_binary",
  event_col   = "y_binary",
  treat_col   = "treat",
  id_col      = "id"
)
#> 
#> [forestsearch] Subgroup Identification Configuration
#>   Outcome type:   binary
#>   Effect measure: OR (Odds Ratio)
#>   Scale:          log (ratio)
#> 
#>   Screening:      OR >= 1.67 (log: 0.5110)
#>   Consistency:    OR >= 1.33 (log: 0.2874)
#>   Consistency rate threshold: 80%
#> 
#>   Interpretation:
#>     Candidates: subgroup OR >= 1.67
#>     Splits:     each split OR >= 1.33
#> 
#> ==============================================================
#>   Search Alignment Diagnostic
#> ==============================================================
#> 
#>   Outcome:    y_binary (binary)
#>   Treatment:  treat
#>   Measure:    Odds Ratio (OR) -- estimator sees Y as-is (no flip)
#> 
#>   ForestSearch searches for:
#>     Subgroups where treat increases P(y_binary=1)
#>     (OR >= threshold on the ORIGINAL outcome scale)
#> 
#>   Thresholds:
#>     Screening: OR >= 1.667 in the candidate subgroup
#>     Consistency: OR >= 1.333 in each bootstrap split
#> 
#>   Variable screening:
#>     LASSO: LASSO screening uses glmnet with family = "binomial (logistic)".
#>     Variables with non-zero coefficients are retained.
#>     GRF:   GRF sees 1-y_binary (flipped for causal_forest).
#>     Positive CATE = treatment REDUCES y_binary = treatment HELPS.
#> 
#>   No alignment concerns detected.
#> ==============================================================

5.1 Examine Result

Examine FS result + subgroup OR fits (click to expand) 
cat("\n=== ForestSearch Result ===\n")
#> 
#> === ForestSearch Result ===
Examine FS result + subgroup OR fits (click to expand) 
if (!is.null(fs_actg$grp.consistency)) {
  # NOTE: for a forestsearch object, the cut expressions defining the
  # identified subgroup live in `grp.consistency$sg.harm` (character
  # vector of factor-level cut names).  `grp.consistency$sg.harm.id`
  # is a different object: a per-subject 0/1 indicator of subgroup
  # membership with length nrow(df).  (For GRF objects, `sg.harm.id`
  # does carry the cut expressions — same name, different semantics.)
  sg <- fs_actg$grp.consistency$sg.harm
  if (!is.null(sg) && length(sg) > 0 && !all(is.na(sg))) {
    cat("Subgroup identified:", paste(sg, collapse = " & "), "\n")

    df_est <- fs_actg$df.est
    in_H  <- df_est$treat.recommend == 0
    in_Hc <- df_est$treat.recommend == 1

    cat(sprintf("  Size(H): %d,  Size(Hc): %d\n",
        sum(in_H), sum(in_Hc)))

    if (sum(in_H) >= 10) {
      fit_H <- glm(y_binary ~ treat, data = df_est[in_H, ],
                    family = binomial)
      or_H <- exp(coef(fit_H)["treat"])
      cat(sprintf("  OR(H):  %.3f\n", or_H))
    }
    if (sum(in_Hc) >= 10) {
      fit_Hc <- glm(y_binary ~ treat, data = df_est[in_Hc, ],
                     family = binomial)
      or_Hc <- exp(coef(fit_Hc)["treat"])
      cat(sprintf("  OR(Hc): %.3f\n", or_Hc))
    }

    fit_itt <- glm(y_binary ~ treat, data = df_est, family = binomial)
    cat(sprintf("  OR(ITT): %.3f\n",
        exp(coef(fit_itt)["treat"])))
  } else {
    cat("No subgroup identified by ForestSearch.\n")
  }
} else {
  cat("ForestSearch did not return grp.consistency.\n")
}
#> Subgroup identified: !{wtkg <= 83.4624} & !{cd40 <= 390} 
#>   Size(H): 83,  Size(Hc): 1000
#>   OR(H):  4.921
#>   OR(Hc): 0.559
#>   OR(ITT): 0.665

5.3 FS vs GRF Concordance on Observed Data

When a method does not detect a subgroup, its classification is “all subjects to \(Q^c\)” (treat.recommend = 1 for everyone). compare_fs_subgroups() handles this automatically — no manual fallback is needed.

  subgroup_notation  = sg_notation,
  title              = "FS vs GRF: Subgroup Membership Concordance",
  subtitle           = "ACTG175 observed data (binary benefit search, raw continuous)",
  font_size          = 13
)

6 Single Trial Simulation

Before the full simulation study, simulate a single replicate from the calibrated DGM and run the two analysis methods end-to-end with details = TRUE. This mirrors what every replicate inside the Monte Carlo loop will see and lets us sanity-check the full pipeline – LASSO screening, GRF pre-screening, candidate enumeration, consistency evaluation, subgroup-effect estimation – before burning the budget of thousands of replicates.

Unlike Section 5, the true subgroup here is known by construction (it is the DGM-embedded Q). Per-replicate classification metrics are reported in aggregate for the full simulation loop in Section 8; here we show only the identified subgroup definitions and estimated ORs so the pipeline can be inspected end-to-end on a single replicate.

Simulate one trial from the calibrated DGM (click to expand)

if (!is.null(fs_single$sg.harm) && length(fs_single$sg.harm) > 0L &&
    !all(is.na(fs_single$sg.harm))) {

  cat("Subgroup identified (cut expressions):\n")
  for (s in fs_single$sg.harm) cat("  ", s, "\n")

  df_est <- fs_single$df.est
  in_H   <- df_est$treat.recommend == 0

  # Subgroup effect on switched and original scales
  if (sum(in_H) >= 10L) {
    fit_H <- glm(y_sim ~ treat_sim,
                 data = df_est[in_H, ], family = binomial)
    or_H  <- exp(coef(fit_H)["treat_sim"])
    cat(sprintf("\n  OR(H_hat, switched) = %.3f  (inverted: %.3f)\n",
        or_H, 1/or_H))
  }
  if (sum(!in_H) >= 10L) {
    fit_Hc <- glm(y_sim ~ treat_sim,
                  data = df_est[!in_H, ], family = binomial)
    cat(sprintf("  OR(Hc_hat, switched) = %.3f  (inverted: %.3f)\n",
        exp(coef(fit_Hc)["treat_sim"]),
        1/exp(coef(fit_Hc)["treat_sim"])))
  }

} else {
  cat("No subgroup identified by ForestSearch on this replicate.\n")
}

7 Running Simulation Studies

7.1 Setup

FS / GRF parameter lists for run_simulation_analysis() (click to expand) 
plan(multisession, workers = n_workers)
cat("Using", n_workers, "parallel workers\n")
#> Using 13 parallel workers
FS / GRF parameter lists for run_simulation_analysis() (click to expand) 
# -- Candidate variable set (RAW continuous + binary) --------------------------
# This is the key behavioural change vs the prior discretised setup:
# forestsearch() and grf.subg.harm.glm() receive raw continuous inputs
# and must discover cuts.
cat("Analysis confounders passed to FS/GRF:\n")
#> Analysis confounders passed to FS/GRF:
FS / GRF parameter lists for run_simulation_analysis() (click to expand) 
cat("  ", paste(confounders_analysis, collapse = ", "), "\n")
#>    age, preanti, wtkg, karnof, cd40, cd80, hemo, homo, drugs, race, gender, symptom
FS / GRF parameter lists for run_simulation_analysis() (click to expand) 
# -- ForestSearch parameters ---------------------------------------------------
fs_params <- list(
  # Column name mappings
  outcome.name           = "y_sim",
  event.name             = "y_sim",
  treat.name             = "treat_sim",
  id.name                = "id",

  # GLM pipeline
  outcome_type           = "binary",
  effect_measure         = "OR",

  # Variable screening
  use_lasso              = fs_use_lasso,
  use_grf                = fs_use_grf,

  # Consistency algorithm (v0.2.0 default: 3-10x speedup)
  use_twostage           = TRUE,

  # Continuous-variable detection threshold
  cont.cutoff            = fs_cont_cutoff,

  # Candidate cut strategy for continuous covariates
  # ("default" = mean + median + Q1 + Q3 per continuous variable;
  #  "median"  = median only). See setup chunk for full explanation.
  cut_type               = fs_cut_type,

  # Subgroup detection thresholds
  # Note: hr.threshold/hr.consistency are the generic ForestSearch
  # parameter names regardless of endpoint type. For binary outcomes,
  # these represent OR thresholds on the switched scale.
  hr.threshold           = fs_or_threshold,
  hr.consistency         = fs_or_consistency,
  pconsistency.threshold = fs_pconsistency,

  # Candidate-selection criterion: "maxSG" prefers the LARGEST
  # candidate subgroup meeting the consistency threshold (see setup
  # chunk for full description of sg_focus options).
  sg_focus               = fs_sg_focus,

  # Computational constraints
  fs.splits              = fs_splits,
  n.min                  = fs_n_min,
  d0.min                 = fs_d0_min,
  d1.min                 = fs_d1_min,
  maxk                   = fs_maxk,
  vi.grf.min             = fs_vi_grf_min,
  dmin.grf               = fs_dmin_grf,   # FS-internal GRF cut filter
  seedit                 = fs_seedit,

  # GRF tuning (applies to ForestSearch's internal GRF pre-screening)
  tune_grf               = grf_tune,

  # Inner parallelism: sequential within each worker
  parallel_args          = list(
    plan = "sequential", workers = 1, show_message = FALSE
  )
)

# -- GRF standalone parameter overrides ----------------------------------------
grf_params <- list(
  dmin.grf     = grf_dmin,
  maxdepth     = grf_maxdepth,
  sg.criterion = grf_sg_criterion,
  tune_grf     = grf_tune
)

7.2 Alternative Hypothesis Simulations

H1 simulation loop — foreach wiring + run_simulation_analysis() (click to expand) 
cat("Running", nsims_alt, "simulations under H1...\n")
if (diag_keep_first_n > 0L) {
  cat(sprintf("  Diagnostic capture: keep = {%s}, first %d sim(s)\n",
      paste(diag_keep, collapse = ", "), diag_keep_first_n))
}
t0 <- proc.time()[3]

results_alt_raw <- foreach(
  sim = seq_len(nsims_alt),
  .errorhandling = "pass",
  .options.future = list(
    packages = c("forestsearch", "survival", "data.table", "future"),
    seed = TRUE
  )
) %dofuture% {
  future::plan("sequential")
  run_simulation_analysis(
    sim_id           = sim,
    dgm              = dgm_calibrated,
    n_sample         = sim_n_sample,
    confounders_base = confounders_analysis,
    n_add_noise      = sim_n_noise,
    run_fs           = run_fs,
    run_fs_grf       = run_fs_grf,
    run_grf          = run_grf,
    fs_params        = fs_params,
    grf_params       = grf_params,
    keep             = diag_keep,
    keep_first_n     = diag_keep_first_n,
    verbose          = FALSE
  )
}

timings$sims_alt <- proc.time()[3] - t0

# Post-hoc failure accounting + diagnostic harvest
# keep_diagnostics = TRUE preserves per-replicate fs_full / candidate_table
# attached by run_simulation_analysis() (stripped by rbindlist otherwise).
results_alt <- collect_results(results_alt_raw, "H1 alt",
                               keep_diagnostics = diag_keep_first_n > 0L)
n_failed_alt <- attr(results_alt, "n_failed")
diagnostics_alt <- attr(results_alt, "diagnostics")

cat("Completed in", round(timings$sims_alt / 60, 1), "minutes\n")
cat("Results:", nrow(results_alt), "rows\n")
if (n_failed_alt > 0) cat(sprintf("  *** %d FAILED ***\n", n_failed_alt))
if (!is.null(diagnostics_alt))
  cat(sprintf("  Diagnostic objects captured: %d replicate(s)\n",
      length(diagnostics_alt)))
if (nrow(results_alt) > 0) {
  cat(sprintf("Detection rate: %.1f%%\n",
      100 * mean(results_alt$any.H[results_alt$analysis == "FS"])))
} else {
  cat("All simulations failed — see error messages above.\n")
  cat("Common causes:\n")
  cat("  1. devtools::document() -> devtools::install() -> restart R needed\n")
  cat("  2. Package version mismatch between interactive and worker sessions\n")
}

7.3 ForestSearch Sensitivity Diagnostic

NoteWhy this section exists

Empirically, FS sensitivity in this configuration hovers around 20%. That raises the question: which subgroups is FS actually identifying? If it consistently picks up one component of the true subgroup \(Q = \{\text{age} > 34 \cap \text{preanti} \le 745\}\) but misses the other, the low sensitivity is mechanical (one-of-two cuts → ≈ 50% true-Q overlap, further diluted by cut-point mismatch). If it picks noise variables, the low sensitivity reflects a different problem. The diagnostics below separate these hypotheses.

7.3.1 Per-replicate subgroup definitions (first 20)

The sg.def column on results_alt carries the cut-expression string of the FS-identified subgroup for every replicate (a v0.2.0 addition to run_simulation_analysis()). We print the first 20 alongside the corresponding sensitivity / PPV / size for context.

7.3.3 Variable-level frequency

Each subgroup definition is a conjunction of one or more cut expressions. Here we parse out the variable names appearing in those cuts and count how often each variable is selected. If FS is recovering one component of true-\(Q\) but missing the other, this table will show a strong imbalance between age and preanti.

Variable-level frequency across FS finds (click to expand) 
extract_vars <- function(sg_str) {
  if (!nzchar(sg_str)) return(character(0))
  parts <- strsplit(sg_str, "\\s*&\\s*", perl = TRUE)[[1]]
  # A cut expression may be wrapped in braces and optionally negated:
  #   "{age <= 34}"       -> variable "age"
  #   "!{age <= 34}"      -> variable "age"
  #   "preanti"           -> variable "preanti"   (plain indicator)
  # Strip the outer !/{ / } wrappers, then take the first whitespace-
  # delimited token — the variable name.
  vars <- vapply(parts, function(p) {
    p <- trimws(p)
    p <- sub("^!", "",  p)           # optional negation
    p <- sub("^\\{", "", p)           # optional opening brace
    p <- sub("\\}$", "", p)           # optional closing brace
    tok <- strsplit(trimws(p), "\\s+", perl = TRUE)[[1]][1]
    if (is.na(tok)) "" else tok
  }, character(1))
  unique(vars[nzchar(vars)])
}

all_var_uses <- unlist(lapply(fs_rows$sg.def, extract_vars))
if (length(all_var_uses) == 0L) {
  cat("No identified subgroups across any replicate.\n")
} else {
  var_freq <- sort(table(all_var_uses), decreasing = TRUE)
  n_detect <- sum(nzchar(fs_rows$sg.def))
  var_df <- data.frame(
    variable       = names(var_freq),
    n_times_used   = as.integer(var_freq),
    pct_of_detects = round(100 * as.integer(var_freq) / n_detect, 1),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  knitr::kable(
    var_df,
    col.names = c("Variable",
                  "Times used",
                  "% of detecting sims"),
    caption = sprintf(
      paste0("Variables appearing in FS-identified subgroups across ",
             "%d detecting replicates (of %d total)."),
      n_detect, nrow(fs_rows)),
    row.names = FALSE,
    align = c("l", "r", "r")
  )
}

7.3.6 Interpretation

Read the four tables above top-to-bottom:

  • If the subgroup-definition frequency shows a handful of recurring cut expressions dominating, FS is converging on a small number of candidates. If one of them matches true-\(Q\) closely (e.g., age <= 34 & preanti <= 745), sensitivity on those sims should be high in the per-sim table.
  • If the variable frequency shows age dominating and preanti rarely present (or vice versa), FS is recovering one component only. Sensitivity of ≈ 0.50 on that sub-population of sims is expected; weighted by the fraction of times both are found, the average lands near 20%. This is a candidate-enumeration issue, not a pathology.
  • If noise variables (noise1, …) show up prominently, the threshold or consistency settings are too permissive for this sample size.
  • If n_passed > 0 is low (say < 30%), the identification threshold fs_or_threshold is binding and the subgroup is being rejected outright in most sims. This would show up as size.H = 0 and any.H = 0L for those replicates in the per-sim table.

The combination of the four tables is enough to pick between these hypotheses without re-running anything.

8 Results

8.1 Metrics Glossary

Classification metrics follow the definitions in León et al. (2024, Section 3) adapted for the benefit search.

8.1.1 Detection

Found (\(\text{any}(Q)\)): proportion of simulations where the method identifies any benefit subgroup (\(\texttt{any.H} = 1\)).

  • Under H1 (alternative): \(Q\) exists with a differential treatment effect. \(\text{any}(Q)\) is detection power.
  • Under H0 (null): \(Q = \emptyset\) and \(Q^c\) is the ITT population. \(\text{any}(Q)\) is the false positive rate (FPR) for falsely declaring that a benefit subgroup exists.

8.1.2 Classification Under H1

Under the alternative, the true benefit subgroup \(Q\) exists (\(Q = \{z_1 = 1 \cap z_2 = 1\}\), prevalence \(\approx 34\%\)) with a genuinely different treatment effect. Following León et al. (2024, Section 3), define for estimated subgroup \(\hat{Q}\):

\[ \text{sens}(\hat{Q}) = \frac{\#\{i \in \hat{Q} \cap Q\}}{\#\{i \in Q\}}, \quad \text{ppv}(\hat{Q}) = \frac{\#\{i \in \hat{Q} \cap Q\}}{\#\{i \in \hat{Q}\}}, \]

with analogous measures for the complement \(\hat{Q}^c\).

The operating-characteristics tables report these as:

Table column León et al. notation Interpretation
Sen \(\text{sens}(\hat{Q})\) Fraction of true \(Q\) captured by \(\hat{Q}\)
Spec \(\text{sens}(\hat{Q}^c)\) Fraction of true \(Q^c\) correctly in \(\hat{Q}^c\)
PPV \(\text{ppv}(\hat{Q})\) Fraction of \(\hat{Q}\) truly in \(Q\)
NPV \(\text{ppv}(\hat{Q}^c)\) Fraction of \(\hat{Q}^c\) truly in \(Q^c\)

Classification metrics are averaged across all simulations (León et al. 2024, Table 1). When no subgroup is detected (\(\hat{Q} = \emptyset\)), the simulation contributes \(\text{sens}(\hat{Q}) = 0\) and \(\text{ppv}(\hat{Q}) = 0\) (since no member of \(Q\) is captured and no subjects are assigned to \(\hat{Q}\)). This convention is implemented at the source in run_simulation_analysis(), matching the original fs.estimates.out() function used in León et al. (2024).

NoteClassification metrics with discovered cuts

Because cuts are discovered from the data in this setup, a \(\hat{Q}\) that captures “roughly the right region” but with slightly shifted boundaries will still receive high sens/PPV. Expect these metrics to be lower than under the discretised (oracle-cut) setup — the gap quantifies the cost of not knowing the true cuts in advance.

8.1.3 Classification Under H0

Under the null, \(Q = \emptyset\) — no subgroup with a differential treatment effect exists. The complement \(Q^c\) is the entire ITT population. Per León et al. (2024, Section 3), \(\text{sens}(\hat{Q})\) is undefined (shown as “—” in the table) and \(\text{ppv}(\hat{Q}) \equiv 0\). For the complement, \(\text{sens}(\hat{Q}^c) = |\hat{Q}^c|/N\) and \(\text{ppv}(\hat{Q}^c) = 1\) since \(Q^c\) = ITT.

The only operationally meaningful metric under H0 is the detection rate (FPR).

8.1.4 Effect Estimates

All effect estimates are displayed on the original treatment scale (OR \(< 1\) = benefit from ZDV+ddI) via subgroup_notation = "benefit".

8.2 Operating Characteristics Under H1

TipInterpreting high Sens / low PPV

The combination of high sensitivity (~85%) with low specificity (~20%) and low PPV (~35%) is internally consistent and follows directly from Bayes’ theorem. The Bayes relationship is:

\[ \text{PPV} = \frac{\text{Sens} \times \pi} {\text{Sens} \times \pi + (1 - \text{Spec}) \times (1 - \pi)} \]

where \(\pi \approx 34\%\) is the true-\(Q\) prevalence. Substituting the observed metrics confirms PPV \(\approx\) 35%. The pattern arises because \(\hat{Q}\) is much larger than \(Q\) — roughly 2–2.5\(\times\) the true subgroup size (check avg\(|\hat Q|\) above). The method recovers most of \(Q\) (high sensitivity) but also absorbs most of \(Q^c\) (low specificity), yielding a “diluted” \(\hat{Q}\) with low purity (PPV). This is expected when cuts are discovered from continuous covariates rather than known a priori; the raw-continuous boundary \(\{z_1 = 1 \cap z_2 = 1\}\) is harder to recover precisely than a discretised oracle-cut design.

8.2.1 True Subgroup Sizes Across Replicates

run_simulation_analysis() records the per-replicate size of the true benefit subgroup \(Q\) (flag_harm == 1) and its complement \(Q^c\) (flag_harm == 0) in the columns sizeH_true, sizeHc_true, propH_true, propHc_true. The estimation tables below report \(\widehat{|H|}\) (the identified subgroup size averaged across replicates); the callout here gives the corresponding true-subgroup sizes for comparison.

Show code 
# One row per replicate-method combination, but sizeH_true is identical
# across method rows within the same sim. Deduplicate on sim.
truth_by_sim <- unique(results_alt[, c("sim", "sizeH_true", "sizeHc_true",
                                        "propH_true", "propHc_true")])

callout_Q <- sprintf(
  "|Q|:  mean = %.1f (SD %.2f),  range = [%d, %d],  prop = %.1f%%",
  mean(truth_by_sim$sizeH_true),
  sd(truth_by_sim$sizeH_true),
  min(truth_by_sim$sizeH_true),
  max(truth_by_sim$sizeH_true),
  100 * mean(truth_by_sim$propH_true))

callout_Qc <- sprintf(
  "|Qc|: mean = %.1f (SD %.2f),  range = [%d, %d],  prop = %.1f%%",
  mean(truth_by_sim$sizeHc_true),
  sd(truth_by_sim$sizeHc_true),
  min(truth_by_sim$sizeHc_true),
  max(truth_by_sim$sizeHc_true),
  100 * mean(truth_by_sim$propHc_true))

            nrow(truth_by_sim), sim_n_sample))

Compare to \(\widehat{|H|}\) (the FS-identified subgroup size) reported in the row-group labels of the estimation tables below. A ratio \(\widehat{|H|} \big/ \overline{|Q|} \approx 1\) indicates the method is recovering a subgroup close to the true size; values much smaller suggest FS is identifying a strict subset of \(Q\); values larger suggest FS is absorbing some \(Q^c\) subjects into \(\hat H\).

8.2.2 Distribution of Identified Subgroups

TipReminder: the true subgroup

The true subgroup \(Q\) that FS is trying to recover is defined by \(\{\text{age} > 34\} \cap \{\text{preanti} \le 744.5\}\).

  • Observed ACTG175 prevalence: 382 / 1083 (35.3%).
  • Simulated-trial prevalence (\(n = 1000\)): mean 344.3 (SD 15.31, range 306–380, proportion 34.4%).

Under H1 the bar chart should concentrate on definitions close to this anchor. Under H0 the true subgroup does not exist, so any finds reflect false discovery across the candidate space.

The distribution of the identified subgroup \(\hat H\) under H1 (calibrated HTE) and H0 (null) is rendered by forestsearch::plot_sg_distribution(). Three vignette-level settings control how the charts behave:

  1. Top-K cap (sgdist_top_k = 15): at most that many bars are shown; additional passing labels pool into a single “Other (k labels)” row (or are suppressed – see sgdist_show_other_alt / sgdist_show_other_null). Without this, a diffuse H0 with one find per distinct label (the textbook false-positive signature) renders as overlapping, unreadable rows.
  2. Auto-halving (max_halvings = 2L): the minimum-percentage thresholds (sgdist_min_pct_alt = 0%, sgdist_min_pct_null = 0%) are halved up to twice if no label clears the initial value, so the chart does not render empty.
  3. Adaptive figure height via sgdist_fig_height(), driven by attr(p, "n_bars"), keeps the vertical resolution consistent across scenarios regardless of how many distinct labels pass the filter.
Build subgroup-distribution plots (click to expand) 
plot_sgdist_alt <- plot_sg_distribution(
  results              = results_alt[results_alt$analysis == "FS", ],
  any_col              = "any.H",
  label_col            = "sg.def",
  min_pct              = sgdist_min_pct_alt,
  top_k                = sgdist_top_k,
  show_other           = sgdist_show_other_alt,
  max_halvings         = 2L,
  bar_label_inside     = TRUE,
  placeholder_on_empty = TRUE,
  title                = "HTE: Subgroups Identified (H-hat)",
  wrap_width           = 30
)

plot_sgdist_null <- plot_sg_distribution(
  results              = results_null[results_null$analysis == "FS", ],
  any_col              = "any.H",
  label_col            = "sg.def",
  min_pct              = sgdist_min_pct_null,
  top_k                = sgdist_top_k,
  show_other           = sgdist_show_other_null,

h_alt  <- sgdist_fig_height(attr(plot_sgdist_alt,  "n_bars"))
h_null <- sgdist_fig_height(attr(plot_sgdist_null, "n_bars"))
Show code 
print(plot_sgdist_alt)
Show code 
print(plot_sgdist_null)

Under sg_focus = "maxSG" and H1, the chart should concentrate on definitions close to the true \(Q\) anchor (age \(> 34\) and preanti \(\le\) 745 on the discretised side of the DGM). Under H0 the find rate is low and any bars that clear the (possibly auto-halved) threshold are scattered across the candidate space — the expected false-discovery signature. When the H0 chart is dominated by a large “Other (k labels)” bar — i.e., many distinct labels each passing the threshold at count 1 or 2 — that is itself the diagnostic: FS is firing on unrelated noise with no preferred label.

8.2.3 Distribution of Effect Estimates

The MRCT analogue is forestsearch::SGplot_estimates(), which displays violins for four populations (ITT, non-AP training, AP testing, AP-subgroup) defined by the train/test split used in the MRCT consistency framework. The ACTG175 binary-benefit study is a single-population design (no train/test split), so we construct a three-panel binary analogue using the columns hr.itt (ITT OR), hr.H.hat (identified subgroup \(\hat H\)), and hr.Hc.hat (identified complement \(\hat H^c\)) that run_simulation_analysis() already populates. All three are on the switched-treatment scale and inverted to the original benefit scale for display. On the benefit scale, OR \(> 1\) indicates the ZDV+ddI combination is superior to ddI monotherapy. As before, both H1 and H0 scenarios are shown.

H1 OR-distribution violin (click to expand) 
or_Q_true <- 1 / dgm_calibrated$hazard_ratios$harm_subgroup

plot_effect_distribution(
  results           = results_alt,
  analysis_method   = "FS",
  effect_measure    = "OR",
  subgroup_notation = sg_notation,
  reference_effect  = or_Q_true,
  ylim              = ordist_ylim,
  title             = "ACTG175 Binary (HTE): OR Estimates Across Simulations",
  subtitle          = sprintf(
    "n = %d, %d sims | dotted green = true OR(Q) on benefit scale = %.2f",
    sim_n_sample, nsims_alt, or_Q_true)
)
H0 OR-distribution violin (click to expand) 
# Under H0 the DGM has no benefit subgroup -- no true-effect reference.
plot_effect_distribution(
  results           = results_null,
  analysis_method   = "FS",
  effect_measure    = "OR",
  subgroup_notation = sg_notation,
  ylim              = ordist_ylim,
  title             = "ACTG175 Binary (Null): OR Estimates Across Simulations",
  subtitle          = sprintf(
    "n = %d, %d sims | no true harm/benefit subgroup; dashed red = OR = 1",
    sim_n_sample, nsims_null)
)

Under H1 (top panel), the left violin (ITT) is centred near the DGM’s implied ITT benefit; the middle violin (\(\widehat{\mathrm{OR}}(\hat H)\)) should concentrate near the dotted green reference line at the true \(\mathrm{OR}(Q)\); the right violin (\(\widehat{\mathrm{OR}}(\hat H^c)\)) shows the residual effect in the complement and should sit near \(\mathrm{OR} = 1\) (i.e., no benefit in \(\hat H^c\) once \(\hat H\) is removed). Under H0 (bottom panel), all three violins should centre near \(\mathrm{OR} = 1\); any concentration away from 1 in the subgroup panels, conditional on a subgroup being found, reflects the selection-driven bias that the bootstrap bias-correction in forestsearch() is designed to correct.

8.2.4 Interpretation

Show code 
interpret_estimation_table(
  results_alt, dgm_calibrated,
  analysis_method = "FS",
  scenario = "alt",
  subgroup_notation = sg_notation

Under the alternative hypothesis (true OR(Q) = 0.5, true OR(Qc) = 1.5), 188 of 200 simulations (94.0%) identified a subgroup using FS. The identified subgroup averaged 353 patients (complement: 647).

The naive OR in the identified subgroup averaged 0.51 (SD = 0.06), corresponding to 2.1% relative bias versus the true OR(Q) = 0.5. In the complement, the estimate averaged 1.56 (4.3% bias vs. true OR(Qc) = 1.5).

time_per_null <- timings$sims_null / nsims_null

proj_null <- time_per_null * prod_null

10 Discussion

10.1 Key Differences from the Survival Simulation

This document mirrors the structure of actg175_simulations_benefit.qmd (survival endpoint) with the following differences:

  1. No censoring: the binary outcome \(I(\text{cd420} > \text{cd40})\) is fully observed, eliminating censoring model complexity.

  2. Package GLM simulation suite: uses generate_glm_dgm(), calibrate_glm_interaction(), and simulate_from_glm_dgm() instead of generate_aft_dgm_flex(), manual grid search, and simulate_from_dgm(). run_simulation_analysis() dispatches automatically based on the "glm_dgm" class.

  3. OR replaces HR: thresholds and reporting use odds ratios on the switched scale. The subgroup_notation = "benefit" inversion applies identically.

  4. No CDE/AHR estimands: these are survival-specific. The binary DGM stores OR-scale effects in the hazard_ratios list for reporting compatibility.

  5. GRF standalone included: the standalone GRF analysis (grf.subg.harm.glm) uses causal_forest() for candidate factor screening and policy trees for subgroup identification.

10.2 Key Difference from the Prior Discretised Setup

The prior version of this document discretised every continuous covariate into a binary factor (using the same cuts that define the true subgroup \(Q\)) before the analysis step. That setup implicitly gives the analysis methods knowledge of the true cutpoints. This document feeds raw continuous covariates (age, preanti, wtkg, karnof, cd40, cd80) to the analysis methods, so the search methods must discover cuts themselves. The DGM construction is unchanged: the true \(Q\) is still \(\{\text{age} > 34\} \cap \{\text{preanti} \leq 744.5\}\) and the calibration targets the same OR(Q).

Expected consequences relative to the discretised run:

  • Lower sensitivity and PPV for both FS and GRF, because discovered cuts will generally differ from the true cuts.
  • Similar or slightly higher FPR for GRF, because the policy-tree search space is larger over continuous inputs.
  • Detection power depends on how closely the median / GRF-derived cuts align with the true cuts.

10.3 Limitations

  • The binary DGM is based on a logistic regression fitted to the observed ACTG175 data. The super-population preserves the empirical covariate distribution but assumes the logistic model is correctly specified.

  • k_inter is a direct additive shift on the log-odds scale for Q members under treatment. Positive values increase the outcome for Q; negative values decrease it.

  • dmin.grf was calibrated on the discretised setup; a fresh calibration run with raw continuous inputs is recommended before production scaling.

10.4 Reloading Saved Results

When save_results = TRUE, the simulation bundle is saved as an .rds file in the _data/ directory. The bundle carries every scalar, list, and object the vignette reads downstream of the simulation run, which makes it straightforward to (a) reload for interactive analysis or (b) split this document into a separate “run” script and a “report” document in the future.

bundle <- readRDS(
  "../_data/actg175_binary_benefit_simulations_rawcont_100alts_100nulls.rds"
)

# -- Core results (data.tables) --------------------------------------------
results_alt  <- bundle$results_alt
results_null <- bundle$results_null

# -- DGM objects (class "glm_dgm") -----------------------------------------
dgm_calibrated <- bundle$dgm_calibrated
dgm_null       <- bundle$dgm_null

# -- Restore ALL vignette-scope scalars consumed downstream of the run -----
# (Assigning locally lets Section 8 chunks run unchanged against the
#  reloaded bundle.)
with(bundle$config, {
  sim_n_sample        <<- n_sample
  nsims_alt           <<- nsims_alt
  nsims_null          <<- nsims_null
  n_workers           <<- n_workers
  confounders_analysis<<- confounders_analysis
  sg_notation         <<- sg_notation
  sgdist_min_pct_alt  <<- sgdist_min_pct_alt
  sgdist_min_pct_null <<- sgdist_min_pct_null
  sgdist_top_k        <<- sgdist_top_k
  sgdist_show_other_alt  <<- sgdist_show_other_alt
  sgdist_show_other_null <<- sgdist_show_other_null
  grf_dmin            <<- grf_dmin
  prod_alt            <<- prod_alt
  prod_null           <<- prod_null
})

timings      <- bundle$timings
n_failed_alt <- bundle$n_failed_alt
n_failed_null<- bundle$n_failed_null

# -- True effects (convenience) --------------------------------------------
bundle$true_effects$or_Q     # OR(Q) on switched scale
bundle$true_effects$or_Qc    # OR(Qc)
bundle$true_effects$or_ITT   # OR(ITT)
bundle$true_effects$k_inter  # calibrated interaction shift

# -- FS / GRF parameter lists (passed to run_simulation_analysis) ----------
bundle$fs_params
bundle$grf_params

# -- Provenance ------------------------------------------------------------
bundle$timestamp         # when the run completed
bundle$R_version         # R version used
bundle$fs_version        # forestsearch version used

# -- Reproduce Section 8 tables with the reloaded objects ------------------
format_oc_results(results_alt,    subgroup_notation = sg_notation, ...)
build_estimation_table(results_alt, dgm = dgm_calibrated,
                        subgroup_notation = sg_notation, ...)

methods <- sort(unique(results_alt$analysis))

summ <- data.frame(Method = methods, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
for (m in methods) {
  ra <- results_alt[results_alt$analysis == m, ]
  rn <- results_null[results_null$analysis == m, ]

  summ$alt_det[summ$Method == m]   <- mean(ra$any.H, na.rm = TRUE)
  summ$null_fpr[summ$Method == m]  <- mean(rn$any.H, na.rm = TRUE)
  summ$alt_sens[summ$Method == m]  <- mean(ra$sens, na.rm = TRUE)
  summ$alt_ppv[summ$Method == m]   <- mean(ra$ppv, na.rm = TRUE)
  summ$se_det[summ$Method == m]    <- mc_se(
    summ$alt_det[summ$Method == m], nrow(ra))
  summ$se_fpr[summ$Method == m]    <- mc_se(
    summ$null_fpr[summ$Method == m], nrow(rn))
}

11.1 FS vs GRF Classification Concordance Across Simulations

Per-subject classification concordance between ForestSearch and GRF is computed within each simulation replicate by run_simulation_analysis() and stored as agree.FS.GRF and kappa.FS.GRF columns. When a method does not detect a subgroup, it classifies all subjects to \(Q^c\).

Classification concordance (click to expand) 
conc_col <- "agree.FS.GRF"
kappa_col <- "kappa.FS.GRF"

if (all(c(conc_col, kappa_col) %in% names(results_alt)) &&
    all(c("FS", "GRF") %in% methods)) {

  # One row per sim (take FS rows — concordance is per-sim, same on both)
  fs_alt  <- results_alt[results_alt$analysis == "FS", ]
  grf_alt <- results_alt[results_alt$analysis == "GRF", ]
  n       <- nrow(fs_alt)

  both     <- sum(fs_alt$any.H == 1 & grf_alt$any.H == 1)
  fs_only  <- sum(fs_alt$any.H == 1 & grf_alt$any.H == 0)
  grf_only <- sum(fs_alt$any.H == 0 & grf_alt$any.H == 1)
  neither  <- sum(fs_alt$any.H == 0 & grf_alt$any.H == 0)
  both_idx <- fs_alt$any.H == 1 & grf_alt$any.H == 1

  conc_df <- data.frame(
    Metric = c(
      "Mean agreement (%)",
      "SD agreement (%)",
      "Mean kappa",
      "SD kappa",
      "Median kappa",
      "Both detect",
      "FS only",
      "GRF only",
      "Neither",
      sprintf("Mean agreement | both detect (n = %d)", both),
      sprintf("Mean kappa | both detect (n = %d)",     both)
    ),
    Value = c(
      sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(fs_alt[[conc_col]],  na.rm = TRUE)),
      sprintf("%.1f", 100 * sd(fs_alt[[conc_col]],    na.rm = TRUE)),
      sprintf("%.3f",       mean(fs_alt[[kappa_col]], na.rm = TRUE)),
      sprintf("%.3f",       sd(fs_alt[[kappa_col]],   na.rm = TRUE)),
      sprintf("%.3f",       median(fs_alt[[kappa_col]], na.rm = TRUE)),
      sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", both,     100 * both     / n),
      sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", fs_only,  100 * fs_only  / n),
      sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", grf_only, 100 * grf_only / n),
      sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", neither,  100 * neither  / n),
      if (both > 0)
        sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(fs_alt[[conc_col]][both_idx],  na.rm = TRUE))
      else "\u2014",
      if (both > 0)
        sprintf("%.3f",         mean(fs_alt[[kappa_col]][both_idx], na.rm = TRUE))
      else "\u2014"
    ),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

  cat(gt::as_raw_html(
    gt::gt(conc_df,
           groupname_col = NULL) |>
      gt::tab_header(title = sprintf(
        "FS vs GRF classification concordance (%d sims)", n)) |>
      gt::tab_row_group(label = "Overall agreement",
                        rows = 1:5) |>
      gt::tab_row_group(label = "Detection patterns",
                        rows = 6:9) |>
      gt::tab_row_group(label = "Conditional on both detecting",
                        rows = 10:11) |>
      gt::row_group_order(groups = c(
        "Overall agreement",
        "Detection patterns",
        "Conditional on both detecting")) |>
      gt::cols_label(Metric = gt::md("**Metric**"),
                     Value  = gt::md("**Value**")) |>
      gt::tab_options(table.font.size = 11)
  ), "\n\n")

} else {
  cat("*Concordance columns not found in results.  Ensure",
      "`run_simulation_analysis()` was called with",
      "`run_fs = TRUE` and `run_grf = TRUE`.*\n\n")
}

12 Appendix: Effect Measures and Outcome Direction Conventions

This appendix is a quick-lookup reference for this vignette’s directional configuration. For comprehensive coverage across all endpoint types – including the eight-scenario decision table, worked code examples for binary, continuous, count, and survival outcomes, common pitfalls, and verification tests – see the standalone ForestSearch Outcome Orientation Reference vignette.

12.1 A.1 The unified harm-search convention

Every subgroup search in forestsearch uses a single comparison direction throughout the pipeline. In each candidate subgroup \(S\), the package checks whether the estimated treatment effect satisfies

\[ \hat{\theta}(S) \;\geq\; c_1 \]

(effect.threshold), with the same direction reused for the bootstrap consistency check, \(\hat{\theta}(S_b) \geq c_2\). This comparison never flips. The entire question of how to set up a search reduces to: how do I orient my data so the subgroup I want to find produces \(\hat{\theta}(S) > 0\) on the chosen effect scale?

Two transformations handle the orientations that don’t satisfy this naturally. First, benefit search – finding a subgroup in which the original experimental treatment is beneficial – is implemented by switching the treatment labels so the worse arm becomes treat = 1. A benefit subgroup of the original experimental then appears as a harm subgroup of the switched-treatment; magnitudes are inverted at reporting time via subgroup_notation = "benefit". Second, when the user’s binary outcome is encoded on the positive scale (higher \(Y\) = better), the binary effect estimator can substitute \(1 - Y\) before computing the OR – this is what the adverse_outcome flag controls in the FS estimator path.

The flag’s name suggests an interpretive label (“the outcome is adverse”), but mechanically what it does in the binary FS estimator is flip \(Y\) to \(1 - Y\) when adverse_outcome = FALSE, and leave \(Y\) as-is when TRUE (the default for binary). The two framings – pre-flip \(Y\) at data prep and pass TRUE, or keep \(Y\) positive and pass FALSE – are mechanically equivalent for binary outcomes. For continuous and count outcomes the FS effect estimator does not auto-flip on the flag (only the GRF candidate-cut step does); for those outcome types you must encode \(Y\) on the harm direction at data prep and pass adverse_outcome = TRUE. The simplest safe rule across all GLM outcome types is therefore: encode \(Y\) on the adverse scale at data prep and pass adverse_outcome = TRUE everywhere. This is the convention used by the present vignette; see Section 1.3 for the specific row that applies and Section 1.1 for the data-prep step.

TipDGM golden rule

Once the data is correctly oriented, build the DGM with positive k_inter, a positive calibration target, and a positive k_inter_range grid. The DGM operates on the final, oriented data; outcome and treatment manipulations (negation, switching) happen at the data-prep step, before the DGM is constructed.

12.2 A.2 Effect scales and threshold conventions

forestsearch works on the log scale internally for ratio measures and on the identity scale for additive measures. This affects how effect.threshold is interpreted:

Measure type Examples What effect.threshold = c₁ becomes
Ratio HR, OR, IRR, RR \(\log(c_1)\) – e.g., 1.25 → 0.223
Additive (bounded) RD, IRD \(c_1\) directly; bounded in \([-1, 1]\)
Additive (unbounded) MD \(c_1\) directly; unbounded

For RD and IRD, the package warns and remaps if the threshold is set outside the bounded range. For MD (mean difference) the threshold is genuinely unbounded – values like 30 cells/\(\mu\)L are legitimate, and the package no longer remaps them as it once did when MD was incorrectly treated as a bounded measure. In all cases, the comparison the package performs internally is \(\hat{\theta} \geq\) (transformed threshold), with \(\hat{\theta}\) on the same scale (log for ratios, identity for additives).

12.4 A.4 Worked example: this vignette’s configuration

The present vignette uses the row Binary | OR | Adverse | Benefit. Concretely:

  • The clinical concept is improvement (CD4 response by 20 weeks), but y_binary is encoded at data prep on the adverse scale as \(I(\text{cd420} \leq \text{cd40})\) – a 1 indicates failure to improve.
  • Treatment is switched so ddI \(\to\) treat = 1 and ZDV+ddI \(\to\) treat = 0.
  • adverse_outcome defaults to TRUE for binary inside forestsearch() and is consistent with the adverse encoding of y_binary.
  • The package’s harm-search machinery flags subgroups where the switched treatment (ddI) increases the odds of non-improvement – equivalently, where the original experimental (ZDV+ddI) is beneficial in giving improvement.
  • Calibration target \(\text{OR}(Q) = 2\) corresponds to a \(2\times\) odds-ratio of benefit for ZDV+ddI in \(Q\). This is the same magnitude as OR computed on the natural (original treatment, improvement-Y) scale, by the \(\text{OR}(\text{switched, adverse}) = \text{OR}(\text{original, positive})\) symmetry.
  • Reporting uses subgroup_notation = "benefit" so summary tables display effect estimates on the original-experimental side.

12.5 A.5 Common pitfalls

The standalone ForestSearch Outcome Orientation Reference is the authoritative source for setup mechanics across all endpoint types. Two pitfalls show up often enough in practice to flag here:

WarningPitfall 1: calibration target on the wrong scale

Setting (e.g.) cal_target_or = 0.5 together with a negative k_inter_range produces a \(Q\) that is only marginally more extreme than the rest of the sample in the same direction – no real contrast. Symptom: near-100% detection paired with very high false-positive rate (~97%). Fix: use a target above 1 with a positive k_inter grid for ratio measures, or a positive target with a positive grid for MD.

WarningPitfall 2: adverse_outcome confused with outcome negation

Setting adverse_outcome = FALSE for a benefit search with switched treatment and a positive binary outcome causes the binary FS estimator to flip \(Y \to 1 - Y\), reversing the OR direction and breaking the \(\hat{\theta} \geq c_1\) comparison. Symptom: zero detection. Fix: leave adverse_outcome at its default TRUE for binary, or pre-flip \(Y\) at data prep (the convention used by this vignette – see Section 1.3).

For the full list of pitfalls – including MD-threshold remapping behaviour, survival with positive events, and DGM construction gotchas – the eight-scenario decision table, the four verification tests, and worked code examples for binary, continuous, count, and survival outcomes, see the standalone ForestSearch Outcome Orientation Reference vignette.
